Source: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for Kindergarten Through 8th Grade (IES What Works Clearinghouse practice guide)
What it says, in our words: Advises building on sharing and using number lines as a main tool for fractions from the early grades.
Where we used it: Zip Line, Number Hop, Slice Shop, Equal Pieces

Source: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (IES What Works Clearinghouse practice guide, 2021)
What it says, in our words: Six recommendations, including concrete and drawn models, number lines, taught word problems, and timed practice for fluency.
Where we used it: The math tools, Story Stage for word problems, Catch It

Source: Foundational Skills to Support Reading for Understanding in Kindergarten Through 3rd Grade (IES What Works Clearinghouse practice guide, 2016)
What it says, in our words: Four recommendations: academic language, sounds and letters, decoding and word parts, and daily reading of connected text with feedback.
Where we used it: Sound Studio, Word Lab, Radio Show, Fix-It Press

Source: Florida Center for Reading Research, Student Center Activities
What it says, in our words: A free bank of pre-K to grade 5 reading activities grouped by phonological awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension.
Where we used it: Used as a checklist of activity types. Nothing was copied.

Source: The Math Learning Center, free math apps
What it says, in our words: Free virtual models such as fractions, geoboard, number line, number frames, number rack, money pieces, and a clock.
Where we used it: Checked our tool list against these

What it says, in our words: A free set of virtual manipulatives including algebra tiles, fraction bars, number lines, dice, spinners, and a balance scale.
Where we used it: Checked our tool list against these

Source: Erroneous examples studies (Adams, McLaren and colleagues, middle school decimals)
What it says, in our words: Finding and fixing a planted error helped on a delayed test in some studies and showed no advantage in another. Students liked it less than plain practice.
Where we used it: Fix-It Press. Mixed evidence, so we use it sparingly and the slip belongs to a character.

Source: Concreteness fading (Fyfe, McNeil, Son, and Goldstone, 2014)
What it says, in our words: A review that recommends starting with concrete material and fading step by step to abstract symbols. A later analysis questions how widely it applies.
Where we used it: Every activity ends with a final check that has no model

What it says, in our words: Students who compared two methods side by side gained more procedural knowledge and flexibility than those who studied them one at a time.
Where we used it: Clash and the side by side comparisons in many reactions

Source: Teachable agents and the protege effect (Chase, Chin, Oppezzo, and Schwartz, 2009)
What it says, in our words: Students worked harder to learn for a character they were teaching than for themselves.
Where we used it: A future "teach the Guide" mode. Not used in this batch.
